content: The administration of metformin, an insulin-sensitizing agent, has been extensively studied in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) undergoing ovulation induction or in vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles. Metformin is known to reduce hyperinsulinemia and suppress excessive ovarian androgen production. These mechanisms suggest that metformin could potentially improve outcomes of assisted reproductive techniques (ART), such as reducing ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) and increasing pregnancy and live birth rates. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of metformin as an adjunctive treatment during IVF or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) in achieving pregnancy or live birth in women with PCOS. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing metformin with placebo or no treatment in women of reproductive age with PCOS, with or without additional infertility factors. The primary outcomes assessed were live birth rates and the incidence of OHSS. A total of 13 RCTs involving 1132 women with PCOS undergoing IVF/ICSI were included in this review. The analysis was stratified based on the type of ovarian stimulation protocol used: long gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist (GnRH-agonist) or short gonadotropin-releasing hormone antagonist (GnRH-antagonist). This stratification was performed to determine whether the type of stimulation protocol influenced the outcomes. In the subgroup using the long GnRH-agonist protocol, the pooled evidence indicated uncertainty regarding the effect of metformin on live birth rates compared to placebo or no treatment. The risk ratio (RR) was 1.30, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.94 to 1.79, based on six RCTs involving 651 women. This suggests that if the live birth rate with placebo or no treatment is 28%, the live birth rate with metformin would range between 27% and 51%. The quality of evidence was rated as low. In the subgroup using the short GnRH-antagonist protocol, only one study reported live birth rates. The findings suggested that metformin may reduce live birth rates compared to placebo or no treatment, with an RR of 0.48 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.79) based on 153 women. This implies that if the live birth rate with placebo or no treatment is 43%, the live birth rate with metformin would range between 13% and 34%. The quality of evidence was also rated as low. Metformin may reduce the incidence of OHSS, with an RR of 0.46 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.72) based on 11 RCTs involving 1091 women. This suggests that for a woman with a 20% risk of OHSS without metformin, the risk with metformin would range between 6% and 14%. The quality of evidence was low. In the long GnRH-agonist protocol subgroup, metformin may increase the clinical pregnancy rate compared to placebo or no treatment, with an RR of 1.32 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.63) based on 10 RCTs involving 915 women. In the short GnRH-antagonist protocol subgroup, the effect of metformin on clinical pregnancy rates was uncertain, with an RR of 1.38 (95% CI 0.21 to 9.14) based on two RCTs involving 177 women. The quality of evidence for this outcome was very low. The effect of metformin on miscarriage rates was uncertain when compared to placebo or no treatment, with an RR of 0.86 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.32) based on eight RCTs involving 821 women. The quality of evidence was low. Metformin may result in an increased incidence of side effects compared to placebo or no treatment, with an RR of 3.35 (95% CI 2.34 to 4.79) based on eight RCTs involving 748 women. The quality of evidence was low. Overall, the quality of evidence ranged from very low to low, with the main limitations being inconsistency, risk of bias, and imprecision. The authors concluded that there is no conclusive evidence that metformin improves live birth rates in women with PCOS undergoing IVF/ICSI. In the long GnRH-agonist protocol, metformin may increase clinical pregnancy rates, but its effect on live birth rates remains uncertain. In the short GnRH-antagonist protocol, metformin may reduce live birth rates, but its effect on clinical pregnancy rates is unclear. Metformin may reduce the incidence of OHSS but is associated with a higher incidence of side effects. The effect of metformin on miscarriage rates remains uncertain.
